info.bio: Quincy Delight Jones, Jr. (Chicago, 14 de marzo de 1933), Quincy Jones, compositor, director, arreglista y productor estadounidense de música. Su ámbito de interés musical abarca el pop y el jazz (swing y bop), con frecuente tendencia a su fusión. Asimismo, es intérprete ocasional de trompeta y piano, y cantante. También está vinculado al mundo del cine produciendo películas y componiendo para ellas. Como productor, es famoso sobre todo por haber sido coproductor de algunos de los álbumes más famosos de Michael Jackson.

scenes.name: The Source, Vibe y la radio universitaria
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Dave Mays fundó The Source en 1988 como boletín de estudiantes de Harvard con Jonathan Shecter, James Bernard y Ed Young; tras Word Up! o Hip Hop Hit List se volvió «la biblia del hip hop» y «la CNN» del género: sus cinco micros eran el sello de oro y la columna Unsigned Hype de Matty C, que escuchaba maquetas a cambio de cintas vírgenes, lanzó a Common, DMX o Wu-Tang (Thirstin Howl III la leyó en Rikers). Con el programa de Stretch Armstrong y Bobbito en la radio de la Universidad de Columbia, eran el filtro de la ciudad. Vibe (Quincy Jones, 1993) fue su rival. Las luchas internas y la crisis del papel la hundieron.

scenes.name: El disco
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Una simulación repetitiva de la crudeza del funk negro, alargada por máquinas y no por músicos que improvisan. Nació en clubes europeos de finales de los sesenta que pinchaban funk original, llegó a Estados Unidos y en 1974 era la moda de la Costa Este: aceleró la destrucción de la sesión en directo, de las bandas y de la grabación con alma, y la música negra se volvió más mecánica y menos significativa. El disco quería bailar sin fin sobre un ritmo único; el funk, levantarse y hacer jam («Freak of the Week»: nada de ese «disco sádico» de un solo golpe). Las bandas de funk lo atacaron («The Undisco Kidd», «Anti-Disco» de Mutiny) o se vendieron: James Brown se proclamó «Original Disco Man», los Ohio Players, los Isley y Earth, Wind & Fire («Boogie Wonderland») cayeron. El grito «Disco sucks» metió en el mismo saco a toda la música negra de baile, y muchas bandas de funk murieron por no vender como el disco.

scenes.name: Jazz-funk y fusión
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Tras la muerte de Coltrane (1967), Miles Davis, Cannonball Adderley, Donald Byrd, Ramsey Lewis, Wayne Shorter, Chick Corea y Herbie Hancock se electrificaron con bajo eléctrico, guitarras, teclados y ritmos de James Brown, y sus bandas empezaron a parecer de R&B; otros siguieron a Ornette Coleman hacia la fusión «técnica». Miles respondió a los puristas que lo que arruina la música es la mala música, no los instrumentos. Hacia 1970 el jazz evolucionaba hacia el funk: un fondo funky con encima la improvisación de músicos formados en el jazz (Kool & the Gang, Earth, Wind & Fire, Ohio Players, los Meters, Funk Inc., Mandrill, War, Tower of Power, los Crusaders, los Headhunters y sobre todo los JB’s). El funk es la última música popular negra tocada por músicos de formación jazzística: «el jazz es el maestro, el funk es el predicador» (James Blood Ulmer).

scenes.name: Las bandas soul y los «supergrupos»
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Tras EWF, Rufus y los Commodores las discográficas querían bandas: la «banda soul», versión blanda de la banda funk, unidades completas que podían soltar un groove monstruoso pero se producían como grupos pop. Los Brothers Johnson, descubiertos por Quincy Jones (el bajo de Louis Johnson), triunfaron con Look Out for #1 y Right on Time; Blam! (1978) fue su último funk antes del disco-pop de Lite Up the Nite. Heatwave, sexteto multirracial de Alemania con Rod Temperton y los Wilder de Dayton; L.T.D. con Jeffrey Osborne; Frankie Beverly y Maze (de Filadelfia a California, apadrinados por Marvin Gaye), cinco discos de oro de funk suave; Rose Royce, el vehículo de Norman Whitfield (Car Wash). Off the Wall (1979) de Michael Jackson unió con Quincy Jones, Temperton y Louis Johnson todos los elementos de moda sin perder el groove. Bill Berry los llamó en Ebony (1978) «supergrupos»: espectáculos de estadio de fervor casi religioso, como las giras Earth de P-Funk que lanzaron a Cameo, Slave, Rick James y Bootsy. En 1980 casi todos se habían deshecho o pasado al pop.

podcast.title: Oscar Nominations (1967)
podcast.body: At the 1967 Academy Awards, Quincy Jones's music was tied to multiple films. His score for *In Cold Blood*, based on Truman Capote's novel, was nominated for Best Original Score, and a song he composed for the Robert Wagner film *Banning*, titled "The Eyes of Love," was nominated for Best Original Song. "At the 1967 Oscars, in fact, Q's music was tied to multiple films."

podcast.title: Brain Aneurysm and Career Shift (1974)
podcast.body: In 1974, Quincy Jones suffered a brain aneurysm, a life-threatening event that caused him to re-evaluate his furious work schedule. After making a full recovery, he decided to cut back on his commitments and focus on fewer projects where he felt he could have the most impact. This period of recovery and re-focus is seen as giving his work greater direction and making him an even bigger presence in the music industry. "After he made a full recovery, he decided to cut back on his schedule and focus on fewer projects where he could have the most impact."

podcast.title: Roots Miniseries Score (1977)
podcast.body: Quincy Jones was invited by author Alex Haley to score the televised adaptation of Haley's acclaimed novel of African American history, *Roots*. The epic 1977 miniseries garnered the highest TV ratings ever recorded to that date, and the project earned Quincy Jones his first Emmy award for his musical contribution. "As for his own recordings, Quincy was invited by the author Alex Haley to score the televised adaptation of Roots, his acclaimed novel of African American History."

podcast.title: Arranger for Jazz Legends
podcast.body: After relocating to New York City and finding immediate work, Quincy Jones quickly demonstrated his great skill in not just playing, but also the ability to transcribe horn parts or charts. While barely out of his teens, he served as an arranger, writing charts for esteemed musicians such as Count Basie, Tommy Dorsey, and Dinah Washington. "He wrote charts for the likes of Count Basie, Tommy Dorsey and Dina Washington, serving as an arranger while barely out of his teens."

For the film's title track, he teamed up with his long-time friend Ray Charles. podcast.title: First Black Major Label Executive
podcast.body: In 1961, impressed with his work for their French subsidiary, Mercury Records promoted Quincy Jones to the title of Vice President at Mercury U.S. This historic appointment made him the first black upper-level executive at a major U.S. recording company. "Mercury Records, impressed with his work for their French subsidiary, promoted Quincy to the title of Vice President at Mercury U.S., making him the first black upper-level executive at a major U.S. recording company."

podcast.title: Hollywood Scoring Career
podcast.body: Starting with the 1965 Sydney Lumet film *The Pawnbroker*, Quincy Jones embarked on a prolific sideline career as a Hollywood score composer. Between 1965 and 1972, he composed more than two dozen soundtracks, averaging two to four scores per year, several of which were acclaimed. "Jones was also pursuing a sideline as a Hollywood score composer."

podcast.title: Influence from TONTO on Production
podcast.body: Quincy Jones was greatly impressed by the TONTO synthesizer and its capabilities. What he learned from Malcolm Cecil and Robert Margouleff's work with the instrument significantly influenced how he produced Michael Jackson's albums, thereby bringing new attention to the potential of electronically generated music. "Quincy Jones loved this thing. What he learned shaped how he produced Michael Jackson's albums and it brought all kinds of new attention to the possibilities of electronically generated music."

podcast.title: Leadership in Jazz Orchestras
podcast.body: Around his 20th birthday, Quincy Jones secured a performing break by joining the brass section of vibraphonist and band leader Lionel Hampton, playing trumpet alongside "Ace Players" Art Farmer and Clifford Brown. Three years later, in 1956, he was playing in the band of legendary trumpeter Dizzy Gillespie, who then chose Quincy to lead a big band of outstanding musicians for a special ensemble. "Q could play very well, but from a very young age he was seen as a leader, straddling the worlds of artist and svengali, the guys who made the music and the ones who made the music happen."

podcast.title: Meeting Michael Jackson on The Wiz Set (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: The production of music for the film adaptation of the Broadway musical *The Wiz* was a project Quincy Jones undertook somewhat begrudgingly as a favor to his friend, film director Sidney Lumet. It was on this film set that Jones met a 20-year-old singer, dancer, and former child star named Michael Jackson, who was playing the Scarecrow. Jackson boldly asked Jones if he would consider producing his first adult solo album, a meeting that would profoundly change both their lives. "And it was on the set of The Wiz that Q met a 20 year old who would change his life, a singer, dancer and former child star who was playing the scarecrow."

podcast.title: Pivotal Figure in Yacht Soul
podcast.body: Quincy Jones's 1978 hit single "Stuff Like That" played a key role in establishing him as a pivotal figure in what would later be termed "Yacht Soul." This R&B offshoot of Yacht Rock utilized many of the same nexus of California session musicians favored by smooth bands like Steely Dan, Toto, and The Doobie Brothers, and this distinct sound would prove pivotal to Jones's career by the 1980s. "Stuff like that peaked at number 21 pop and helped establish Jones as the pivotal figure in what would later be termed Yacht Soul."

podcast.title: Relationship with Ray Charles
podcast.body: Quincy Jones and Ray Charles met in the 1940s when Jones was 14 and Charles was 16. Ray Charles served as a formative influence on the younger Quincy, and by the 1950s, with Charles established as an R&B chart-topper, Jones began arranging his albums, including *The Great Ray Charles* (1956) and *The Genius of Ray Charles* (1957), which helped establish Jones as a hitmaker. "16-year-old Ray was a formative influence on 14-year-old Quincy, and by the 50s, with Charles established as an R&B chart-topper, Jones began arranging his albums."

podcast.title: Seattle & Musical Development
podcast.body: In his teens, Quincy Jones's father moved the family to Seattle, Washington, where Quincy continued to pursue his passion for music. He sang with a local gospel troop and learned to play the trumpet in high school, showing enough promise to earn a scholarship to Boston's Schillinger House (later known as the Berklee School of Music) just one year after graduating. "By his teens, Quincy's father had moved the family to Seattle where Quincy pursued his passion for music."

xref.title: Influence on Black Pop and Quincy Jones
xref.body: Malcolm Cecil and Robert Margouleff's work with TONTO, particularly on Stevie Wonder's albums, changed the direction of Wonder's career and redefined what Black Pop music could be. Quincy Jones was highly impressed by TONTO, and what he learned from it shaped how he produced Michael Jackson's albums, drawing new attention to the possibilities of electronically generated music. "Tonto changed the direction of Stevie Wonder's career. And he changed what Black Pop music could be. Quincy Jones loved this thing. What he learned shaped how he produced Michael Jackson's albums and it brought all kinds of new attention to the possibilities of electronically generated music."
